prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Anyone who begins a sentence with, “In all honesty ... ” is about to tell a lie. Anyone who says, “This is how I feel” had better love form more than disclosure. Same for anyone who thinks he thinks well because he had a thought. If you say, “You’re ugly” to an ugly person — no credit for honesty, which must always be a discovery, an act that qualifies as an achievement. If you persist you’re just a cruel bastard, a pig without a mirror, somebody who hasn’t examined himself enough. A hesitation hints at an attempt to be honest, suggests a difficulty is present. A good sentence needs a clause or two, interruptions, set off by commas, evidence of a slowing down, a rethinking. Before I asked my wife to marry me, I told her I’d never be fully honest. No one, she said, had ever said that to her. I was trying to be radically honest, I said, but in fact had another motive. A claim without a “but” in it is, at best, only half true. In all honesty, I was asking in advance to be forgiven.

prompts.L3:
Please expand the following bullet points into a complete, well-structured text:

- Phrases such as “In all honesty” or “This is how I feel” often disguise dishonesty or prioritize form over genuine disclosure.
- Honesty requires discovery and self-examination, not merely stating an obvious or hurtful truth.
- Hesitation, complexity, and revision in speech can signal a sincere effort to be honest.
- Any claim without qualification or contradiction is likely to be only partially true.
- The narrator’s promise never to be fully honest was itself a bid for advance forgiveness rather than an act of radical honesty.
prompts.L4:
Please expand the following two-sentence summary into a complete text:

Honesty is portrayed not as blunt disclosure but as difficult self-examination, pursued through hesitation, qualification, and complex sentences that reveal mixed motives. The narrator’s admission that he could never be fully honest ultimately exposes his request for preemptive forgiveness, showing that truth is partial and genuine honesty requires recognizing contradiction.
prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Anyone, This, Same

outputs.L1:
Anyone who begins a sentence with “In all honesty...” is about to tell a lie. Anyone who says, “This is how I feel,” had better love form more than disclosure. The same applies to anyone who believes he thinks well simply because he has had a thought. If you say, “You’re ugly,” to an ugly person, you deserve no credit for honesty, which must always involve discovery—an act worthy of being called an achievement. If you persist, you are merely a cruel bastard, a pig without a mirror, someone who has not examined himself closely enough.

Hesitation hints at an attempt to be honest; it suggests the presence of difficulty. A good sentence needs a clause or two, interruptions set off by commas—evidence of slowing down, of reconsideration. Before I asked my wife to marry me, I told her I would never be fully honest. No one, she said, had ever told her that. I said I was trying to be radically honest, but in fact I had another motive. A claim without a “but” in it is, at best, only half true. In all honesty, I was asking in advance to be forgiven.
outputs.L2:
The phrase “In all honesty …” usually announces that a falsehood is coming. Likewise, a person who declares, “This is how I feel,” should care more about shaping the statement than about revealing anything. The same applies to someone who mistakes having a thought for thinking intelligently.

Calling an unattractive person ugly earns no praise for candor. Honesty should uncover something; it should require enough effort to count as an accomplishment. Continue with such remarks, and you are merely a cruel bastard—a pig who owns no mirror and has done too little self-examination.

Pausing, by contrast, signals that someone may be struggling toward the truth. A strong sentence contains subordinate turns and comma-bracketed disruptions: signs that the speaker has slowed down and reconsidered. Before proposing to my wife, I warned her that complete honesty from me would never be possible. She replied that nobody had ever told her such a thing. I claimed I was attempting an extreme kind of truthfulness, though I actually had an ulterior purpose. Any assertion that contains no “but” is, in the most favorable case, only partly true. To be honest, I was seeking forgiveness beforehand.
outputs.L3:
Phrases such as “In all honesty” or “This is how I feel” often create the appearance of candor without guaranteeing genuine disclosure. They can function as rhetorical shields, allowing a speaker to present a carefully chosen statement as authentic simply because it is framed as personal truth. In this way, the form of honesty may take precedence over honesty itself. A blunt confession can still conceal motives, omit relevant facts, or protect the speaker from deeper scrutiny.

Real honesty requires more than stating an obvious, convenient, or hurtful truth. It depends on discovery and self-examination: the difficult process of questioning one’s motives, recognizing contradictions, and confronting what one would prefer not to know. A statement is not necessarily honest merely because it is painful to hear. Indeed, cruelty can masquerade as candor when the speaker uses “truth” to avoid empathy or responsibility.

For this reason, hesitation and revision should not automatically be treated as signs of deception. Pauses, qualifications, and changes in wording may reflect a sincere attempt to describe something complicated with greater accuracy. Honest speech often emerges unevenly because people do not always understand their feelings before they begin to express them. The struggle to find the right words can therefore be evidence of integrity rather than evasion.

By contrast, claims that contain no qualification, tension, or contradiction are likely to be only partially true. Human motives and experiences are rarely simple enough to fit into absolute declarations. A statement that sounds perfectly certain may achieve clarity only by excluding inconvenient details. Fuller honesty often requires acknowledging competing impulses: love mixed with resentment, generosity with self-interest, or confidence with fear.

Seen in this light, the narrator’s promise never to be fully honest was not itself an act of radical honesty. Instead, it was a request for forgiveness made in advance. By announcing the inevitability of concealment, the narrator attempted to lower expectations and escape future accountability. The confession did not eliminate dishonesty; it sought permission for it. What appeared to be courageous self-knowledge was therefore another carefully managed form of self-protection.
outputs.L4:
Honesty is portrayed not as the simple act of stating facts, but as a difficult process of self-examination. The narrator does not speak with blunt certainty; instead, his account is marked by hesitation, qualification, and repeated reconsideration. His long, complex sentences suggest a mind struggling to separate sincere feeling from self-interest. As he revises and complicates his claims, he reveals that his motives are mixed: he wants to confess, but he also wants to control how his confession will be received. The form of his speech therefore reflects the moral difficulty of honesty itself. Truth emerges gradually, through uncertainty and contradiction, rather than through a single clear declaration.

This tension becomes most apparent when the narrator admits that he could never be fully honest. On the surface, the admission seems to undermine everything he has said. Yet it may also be his most truthful statement, because it acknowledges the limits of his own perspective. At the same time, the confession serves another purpose: it becomes a request for preemptive forgiveness. By admitting his dishonesty in advance, the narrator asks others to excuse his failures and to judge him sympathetically. His apparent self-criticism is thus both genuine and self-protective.

The passage ultimately suggests that truth is always partial, especially when people attempt to explain their own behavior. Individuals may sincerely seek honesty while still shaping their stories to defend themselves, gain sympathy, or avoid judgment. Genuine honesty, then, does not require perfect transparency, which may be impossible. Instead, it begins with recognizing contradiction: the desire to tell the truth can coexist with the desire to conceal, justify, or be forgiven. The narrator’s struggle is meaningful precisely because he does not resolve these competing impulses. His uncertainty reveals that honesty is less a final achievement than an ongoing willingness to confront the uncomfortable complexity of one’s motives.
outputs.L5: Anyone can begin again. This moment may look like countless others, but it carries its own possibilities. We may walk the same road, face the same doubts, and ask the same questions, yet each step can lead to something new. What matters is choosing to move forward—even when no one knows exactly where the path will end.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a witty, reflective literary passage about honesty, self-deception, and the importance of hesitation and qualification in truthful speech. Include a personal anecdote about proposing to a wife.
counterfactuals.output:
Honesty is often mistaken for a door slammed decisively. In fact, it is more like entering a dark room with one hand extended, saying, “I believe the chair is over here,” and being prepared to revise the sentence after striking one’s shin.

I learned this when I proposed to the woman who became my wife. I had rehearsed a speech of magnificent certainty: *I have never doubted; I have always known; you are the answer to every question.* It was eloquent, polished, and almost entirely false. I had doubted. I had not always known. Some of my questions concerned money, mortality, and whether anyone should be allowed to whistle before breakfast, none of which she answered.

So when the moment came, I hesitated. She watched me kneel and asked whether I had dropped something.

“My nerve,” I said. Then, after a pause: “But perhaps not permanently.”

What I finally told her was that I loved her as honestly as I knew how; that I expected to fail at understanding her; that I hoped to become less foolish in her company; and that, unless she had discovered a compelling objection, I would be delighted to spend my life revising myself beside her.

She said yes—though not before asking what I meant by “compelling.”

That qualification has served us better than all the grand absolutes I had prepared. Self-deception speaks fluently and without commas. Truth clears its throat. It says *perhaps*, *as far as I can tell*, *I may be wrong*. These are not always evasions. Sometimes they are the small hinges on which sincerity turns.

The liar’s favorite costume is certainty, especially certainty about himself. An honest person, by contrast, occasionally stops mid-sentence to inspect the speaker. Hesitation is not the enemy of truth. Often it is truth arriving carefully, wiping its shoes before it enters.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a short philosophical essay arguing that bluntness is not the same as honesty and that genuinely honest statements often require clauses, interruptions, and the word “but.”
counterfactuals.output:
Bluntness is often mistaken for honesty because it arrives without decoration. It sounds fearless: a clean sentence, a hard verdict, an unsoftened fact. Yet removing nuance does not necessarily reveal the truth. Sometimes it merely removes the parts of truth that are inconvenient.

Honesty requires fidelity not only to what we feel, but to the complexity of what is. A person can be irritating and generous, mistaken and perceptive, guilty and forgivable. To say only one of these things may be blunt, but it is not fully honest. Bluntness prefers the straight line; honesty must often follow the crooked shape of reality.

That is why genuinely honest statements tend to gather clauses. They pause, qualify themselves, and interrupt their own momentum: “I love you, but I am angry”; “I understand why you did it, though I cannot excuse it”; “This failed—not entirely, and not for lack of effort—but it failed.” Such sentences may sound hesitant. In fact, their hesitation is a form of courage. They resist the pleasure of certainty long enough to admit competing truths.

The word “but” is especially important. It does not always cancel what came before; often it protects the sentence from becoming a lie. It marks the point where a simple judgment encounters a complicated world.

Bluntness says, “Here is what I think.” Honesty asks, “Is what I think large enough to contain what is true?” The second question takes longer to answer. It may stammer. It may revise itself. But its difficulty is not weakness. It is the sound of conscience making room for reality.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an aphoristic prose piece beginning with the idea that anyone who says “In all honesty” is probably about to lie. Use a caustic, self-aware narrator and end by returning ironically to that phrase.
counterfactuals.output:
Anyone who says “In all honesty” is probably about to lie. Honesty does not require a ceremonial entrance; it comes in through the kitchen, muddy and uninvited. Only deceit rings the bell, wipes its shoes, and presents references.

I know this because I have spent years refining my sincerity. I can lower my voice at will. I can pause before difficult nouns. I can gaze into the middle distance as if truth were grazing there. These are not gifts, exactly, but they have served me better than virtue.

People claim they want candor. What they want is flattery without fingerprints. Tell a man he is brave and he will forgive your accuracy about everything else. Tell a woman she is perceptive and she may not notice you have explained her own life to her. We exchange compliments the way nervous governments exchange hostages.

The plain speaker is merely a tactless liar who has mistaken cruelty for evidence. The diplomat, meanwhile, is a liar with napkins. Between them stands the honest person, despised by both and rarely invited back.

I have tried honesty. Once, at dinner, I answered a question as asked. The silence that followed had weight, architecture, municipal boundaries. Since then I have respected civilization. Civilization is the agreement to say “How interesting” when what we mean is “Please stop,” and “We must do this again” when we mean “After one of us is dead.”

Still, every lie contains a little prayer: let reality be negotiable. Sometimes it is. A marriage can survive on strategic blindness; a career is often built from adjectives no one audits. Even self-knowledge, that stern little idol, depends on flattering light. Strip away every illusion and you do not become wise. You become cold.

So I no longer condemn dishonesty. Condemnation is vanity wearing judicial robes. I merely observe, with the tenderness of a snake regarding a mouse, that we lie most elaborately when we wish to be believed by ourselves.

And I, naturally, am different. I have confessed my methods, exposed my tricks, and made a virtue of admitting I have none. You may trust me.

In all honesty.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a first-person literary monologue on why complete honesty is impossible. Contrast cruel “truth-telling” with honest self-examination, and include dialogue between the narrator and his future wife.
counterfactuals.output:
I used to believe honesty was a clean blade.

I admired people who claimed to wield it without trembling. They said, *I only tell the truth*, and I mistook their lack of mercy for courage. They entered rooms like surgeons who had forgotten the difference between an operation and a wound. A friend showed them a painting; they called it mediocre. A sister wore a new dress; they told her it made her look old. Someone confessed a hope, still frail and translucent, and they crushed it beneath the heel of their judgment.

When the injured protested, these people lifted their hands.

“Would you rather I lied?”

As if those were the only choices: cruelty or deceit. As if silence, patience, tact, uncertainty, and love had never been invented.

I know this because I was one of them.

Years ago, before I learned to distrust the pleasure of being right, I told a woman I did not love her. That much was true. Then I told her I had never loved her, that I had stayed because I was lonely, that her tenderness had become a burden, that even her grief exhausted me. I emptied every locked drawer in my mind and called the wreckage honesty.

For a long time I congratulated myself. I had not deceived her. I had spoken plainly.

Only later did I admit that I had wanted to punish her for needing an explanation I could not give. The “truth” had been my weapon, but the anger behind it had worn a mask. I had confessed her weaknesses and concealed my motive. It was not honesty. It was revenge with good grammar.

That discovery should have humbled me. Instead, for a while, it merely taught me to lie more elegantly.

By the time I met the woman who would become my wife, I had grown wary of declarations. We were sitting in a nearly empty café, late in winter. Outside, snow gathered in the black seams of the pavement. She held her cup in both hands and watched me with the steady expression that would one day frighten doctors, contractors, school principals, and me.

“Tell me something completely true,” she said.

“About what?”

“About yourself.”

I smiled. “Completely?”

“Yes.”

“I don’t think that’s possible.”

“That sounds convenient.”

“It is convenient. That doesn’t make it false.”

She leaned back. “Try.”

So I told her I was afraid she would leave me.

She considered this. “Is that true?”

“Yes.”

“Completely?”

I looked through the window. Our reflections floated over the snow, two pale ghosts seated opposite each other.

“No,” I said. “Part of me is afraid you’ll stay.”

She laughed once—not kindly, but not cruelly either. “Better.”

“And part of me wants you to leave,” I continued, “so I can be proved right about people.”

Her laughter disappeared.

“And part of me wants you to stay so I can be proved right about myself.”

“Which part is the real one?”

“All of them.”

“That’s cheating.”

“Then the truth cheats.”

She was silent for a while. A waiter stacked chairs around us. Somewhere behind the counter, a glass broke, followed by a curse.

At last she said, “Maybe complete honesty isn’t saying everything.”

“What is it, then?”

“Not pretending you know which part is final.”

I remember that sentence because I have been failing to live up to it ever since.

The trouble with complete honesty is not merely that other people cannot bear it. That is the vanity of the self-proclaimed truth-teller: he imagines his soul contains some unbearable radiance, and everyone else must squint. The deeper trouble is that I cannot bear myself clearly enough to report myself without error.

I revise while remembering. I perform while confessing. Even alone, I choose words that make me appear tragic rather than petty, wounded rather than envious, complicated rather than wrong. My mind is both witness and defense attorney. By the time I say, “Here is what happened,” desire has moved the furniture, shame has dimmed the lamps, and pride has opened a window so it can escape.

Complete honesty would require a complete self—a fixed country with surveyed borders. But I am weather. I am argument. I am a house in which every room tells a different story about the fire.

Years after that night in the café, my future wife and I were lying awake in the apartment we would soon leave for a larger one. We had been arguing. I no longer remember why. This, too, is suspicious.

“You’re being honest,” she said into the dark, “but you’re not examining yourself.”

“What’s the difference?”

“Honesty is saying you’re angry.”

“I am angry.”

“Examination is asking what the anger is protecting.”

I wanted to tell her that this sounded like something printed on a therapist’s wall. I wanted to say she was avoiding the issue. I wanted, above all, to win.

Instead I lay still and listened to the small machinery of the building: pipes ticking, a radiator sighing, footsteps crossing the ceiling above us.

Finally I said, “I think I’m ashamed.”

“Of what?”

“I don’t know.”

“That,” she said, “I believe.”

It was the kindest answer she could have given me. She did not demand revelation on schedule. She did not mistake uncertainty for evasion. She let the unknown remain unknown without calling it a lie.

Cruel truth-telling points outward. It names, judges, exposes. It delights in the nakedness of others while remaining fully dressed. Honest self-examination is slower and less theatrical. It begins with suspicion toward one’s own certainty. It asks not only, *Is this statement accurate?* but *Why do I need to say it? Why now? What am I hoping it will do?*

I still lie. I omit, soften, exaggerate, forget. Sometimes I do so from cowardice. Sometimes from kindness. Often I cannot tell the difference until years later, when some old sentence returns with its hidden blade shining.

So I no longer promise complete honesty. That promise is itself dishonest.

What I can promise is to distrust the truth when it makes me feel powerful. I can pause when candor begins to taste like victory. I can turn the blade inward—not to punish myself, but to examine the hand holding it.

And when my wife asks, “Is that really what you feel?”

I can say, “It is what I feel now.”

Then, if I am brave enough, I can add:

“But stay with me. There may be more.”
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a polished paragraph in the style of a contemporary personal essayist, mixing provocative generalizations, dark humor, grammatical observations, and a confession that a promise of radical honesty was really a request for advance forgiveness.
counterfactuals.output: Every relationship begins with a grammatical error: we speak in the future tense as if it were evidence. People say *I will never lie to you* with the same confidence they say *the plane will land safely*, although both claims depend on machinery they neither understand nor maintain. Love, in this sense, is less a feeling than a reckless use of the auxiliary verb. I used to advertise myself as “radically honest,” a phrase that made cruelty sound like an artisanal product, ethically sourced and expensive. The truth is darker and more ordinary: my honesty was selective, my radicalism mostly decorative, and the promise itself was not a promise at all. It was a waiver. I was asking to be forgiven in advance for every confession I intended to mistake for courage, as if naming the body might absolve me of the murder.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
